Justice Sotomayor: Stop Bending the Constitution to Favor Cops

The only problem I have with this headline is that it leaves out the objections by Chief Justice Roberts, as well as Justices Breyer and Kagan. Their remarks are mentioned/quoted in the body of the article, however.

It appeared to me that Roberts was okay with the dog search, despite making this revealing quote to imply otherwise. Maybe that is why Sotomayor is in the headline and Roberts is not. We will see when the decision comes down. There is a good chance for a 5-4 decision here.

Many of the Justices were focused on two things.

  1. What sets this dog sniff apart from other police tasks already allowed?

  2. How much time can be spent to add-on tasks at a road stop?

On the first, there was a general view from Justices including Roberts that running a background check was already not related to the mission of a road stop but it was widely accepted anyway. I would put it this way: the Fourth Amendment was already broken so let's just finish breaking it into utter meaninglessness.

On the second, the focus on the amount of time implied a willingness to allow Constitutional violations if they were short. Antonin Scalia was particularly vocal in implying that a short Constitutional violation may be just fine.

For his part, the defense attorney had much difficulty answering questions. He kept repeating a very general rule about the 'scope of the mission.' Despite repeated inquiries, he could not distinguish these well-accepted police tasks from the additional task of a dog sniff. He under emphasized the fact that the police officer said the mission was done but then decided upon the dog search afterward. I may have pushed that by saying something like, "Perhaps it is difficult to know exactly where Fourth Amendment reasonableness ends. But in this case, we have the officer saying the stop is done. A search after that statement falls well outside of reasonableness."

I would also have explained that a dog sniff was even further away from the reason for the road stop than the background check, as the background check reflects upon the driver exercising his 'privilege' to drive and may be an officer safety concern, whereas a dog sniff does not.

IMNSHO, the government's attorney had trouble answering questions, because it's difficult to justify bringing in the sniffer dogs when the officer had already issued the warning and the reason for the stop ("the mission") was complete. It was an overstep, period.

That said, I believe you are correct, and that it's likely to be a split decision, when it really shouldn't be. Again, in my not so humble opinion. :)

I do not think that the law is favoring police officers; rather it seems to me that the police have found a loophole in search and seizure and are probably abusing such. What loophole that is? The 4th amendment (and I'm heavily paraphrasing because I'm not a fucking dictionary) that searches are to either be conducted with reasonable suspicion or via warrant.

Therefore by using K9 dogs, police are granting themselves an easier path towards reasonable suspicion by supplying themselves knowledge that it is reasonable that there may be drugs.

Police officers are allowed to arrest on this principle and are allowed to intervene in the process of a crime.

The true problem is that the use of K9 dogs for traffic stops is plainly unethical. Traffic cops should be more concerned with upholding the laws of traffic control rather than playing guess-and-check games with small-time drug offenders.
